item.title: My Website
item.description: I've been working a lot on this website over the last few years in terms of both content and features. I think I may have finally reached a landmark where I don't have much left to do in terms of features.
item.content:encoded:
I've been working a lot on this website over the last few years in terms of both content and features. I think I may have finally reached a landmark where I don't have much left to do in terms of features.

That's not to say I won't find excuses to tinker with and improve the site more in the future. But I think I may have ticked every box that I intended to. This website does everything that a blogging website ought to now, or at least, everything that I had any interest in learning and/or implementing.

Now, there is always improvements that can be made. And while I'm happy with the style and structure of my website now, I may change my mind or decide I want to try something new later on down the line. I watch other tech bloggers who seem to enjoy revamping their entire CSS folder periodically. I think that's great, they clearly enjoy digging into the grit and playing with it. I'm quite lazy in that respect. Less is more: it might be more of an excuse than an ethos in my case. Nonetheless, I do prefer to keep things simple whenever I am able to do so. I used to draw a lot, and I really got in to simple yet detailed India ink drawings, with just one or two water colour pencils washed in to a few select parts of a drawing to make it pop. I do like simplicity.

The main reason I started this website was specifically the guides section. Where I log things that I've worked on that don't already have a simple-to-follow guide that I've been able to find. Lots of things I work on do have guides, so naturally the post cycle in that section can sometimes be a little slow — so I added the tech section to add a little meat to the site. I'm glad I pulled the blog section in to this site instead of keeping it on a different site; I didn't really think I'd have much to blog about originally so I thought I'd keep it as an isolated project for a little while. But as it turns out I enjoy writing and it helps me organise my thoughts. For some extra code-centric content I'm thinking I may blog about some specific features of this site that I particularly like. But that will happen as and when, and now that I have this project at a place that I'm happy with I'm going to concentrate on some other things for a little while.

I will still be uploading content here, but I want to get back to learning PHP — which itself may lead to an overhaul of this site's build code. Some bloggers like making things look good, I like making things work good. And also I barely started learning PHP before I got excited and built myself an entire CMS with it, so I don't doubt that there's a lot of improvements that can be made to my codebase. I've also had a pin in learning about iCal and ICS. I know, super nerdy. I really like learning about the lesser thought-of components that make the internet such a useful and interesting tool, and learning the RSS 2.0 spec and figuring out how to implement it from scratch in my website might be one of the most enjoyable things I've done at a computer. There are tools to do it for you, but that's just not what I'm here for, I want to get my hands dirty and enjoy myself!

item.title: I Had A Job Interview
item.description: I had a job interview. Despite my hobbies and the main themes of this website, I do not work in tech. I manage a youth centre — or rather, I am an assistant manager at a youth centre.
item.content:encoded:
I had a job interview. Despite my hobbies and the main themes of this website, I do not work in tech. I manage a youth centre — or rather, I am an assistant manager at a youth centre.

I'm not entirely sure if I want to leave. On reflection, a lot of people have been experiencing big life changes around me: family moving out of London to various places on the Southern coast, friends moving house or out of their parents places for the first time, people getting married, changing careers. Maybe this all got me feeling as though I might benefit from a change too.

I didn't realise until I saw a photograph of myself at work and saw the date stamp in the picture's metadata, but I've been working here for 10 years. I've been working in current role for 6 years. The time has flown past. I enjoy what I'm doing, I find the odd challenge in what I do and on top of that the work is very rewarding.

The job I applied for manifested itself at a fortuitous time; I had been looking at vacancies elsewhere, looking for a new challenge but not being wholly convinced by anything that I was seeing, when the step up from my job (youth centre manager, as opposed to youth centre assistant manager) was advertised for another youth centre in the same area where I work. And it's a 4-6 month placement, with the option to return to my current job at the end of it. It's like the gods of indecision were really pulling every string to get me to go for this.

Obviously, I couldn't ignore the opportunity. I'm still in two minds about the job, and about leaving my current job. And I'm worried that maybe I am only looking for something new because everyone making changes around me is making me feel like I should. But I should, I know I should. My job has become, for the most part, easy. Not in bad way, my work is still rewarding, but I could do perhaps 90% of my job now without really having to think about it.

I have a few days booked off work now. I booked them off to help my mum move to the coast, but she's had to reschedule, so I'm going to take a few days for myself. When I come back from my time off, the emails will have been sent to say whether or not I have the job. The way everything is landing really feels like the universe might be interfering here, and hopefully for the better. I didn't get much time to prepare for the interview originally, as I was helping my sister move to a different part of the coast a few weeks ago, but then the interviews were rescheduled to give me just enough time to prepare and rehearse answers to common interview questions.

I've been hearing that I made a good impression. Even though it was an internal vacancy, I took the interview seriously and tried to put my best self forward. There are eventualities that I can imagine that mean I don't get it, and I'm okay with that. But if I'm being honest with myself, I think the job is going to be hard, and that's what I want. I think I do want this job...

item.title: Do We Really Need Icons?
item.description: I added buttons to copy this sites RSS feed URL's recently. I just threw it together quickly and put "add user feedback" on my to-do list. As is the done thing, I used a nice looking copy icon from the material icon set by Google Fonts. That's the way it's done, I've seen it a million times already, no arguments from me. I've been crossing some of the small tasks off my to-do list this week. I made it to the copy button user feedback in my to-do notes file, and while I was working through the task, I began to have second thoughts about the entire design choice.
item.content:encoded:
I added buttons to copy this sites RSS feed URL's recently. I just threw it together quickly and put "add user feedback" on my to-do list. As is the done thing, I used a nice looking copy icon from the material icon set by Google Fonts. That's the way it's done, I've seen it a million times already, no arguments from me. I've been crossing some of the small tasks off my to-do list this week. I made it to the copy button user feedback in my to-do notes file, and while I was working through the task, I began to have second thoughts about the entire design choice.

After adding the icons and a very rushed animation to indicate that a clicking of an icon had indeed happened, I intended to switch the copy icon to a success tick with a timeout, and add nested div with an attribute of popover with a corresponding value of hint. All very standard stuff, and also ubiquitous. If you haven't coded this yourself, there can be little doubt that you have encountered it many, many times. It's just the done thing. The HTML for the tooltip popover hints had impressed me, I did wonder why there isn't a native popover element, but the existing standards do make a div extremely versatile for this purpose, simply using attributes.

However, as soon as I started with JavaScript I began to lose heart. For however seamless the HTML appeared to be, the JavaScript was anything but. To attach a tooltip to a button, I had to write no less than 4, that's four, event listeners just to achieve basic hover and focus functionality. That is before adding in any conditional logic or anything else. I reconsidered what it was I was trying to achieve...

I had used icons in place of text, mainly to reduce visual clutter. But I think there's also an assumption that icons are the "universal language" - even though the standard paste from clipboard button icon has changed enough times in my lifetime that if I see a copy icon and a paste icon next to each other with no additional context, I have to actually think about which is which. They are not necessarily universal without context. If I showed 50 icons to my dear, old mother, and asked her to guess what each one means, I don't think she'd get even 10 of them correct. They might be language-agnostic (in the global sense, not the coding sense), but icons certainly do rely on context - especially as they become more and more simple in design. I'd argue it is contextual understanding that allows the icon to even exist in the first place.

That's not to say icons are just bad. When using Google Maps to get directions for example, it is quite obvious that the button with the car icon will give you directions for driving and the bicycle icon will give you directions for cycling. But for something that is a concept with no physical representation, such as copy or paste, icons become more ambiguous. It would be proper to provide a tooltip hint for such an icon. Or, stay with me here, we just don't use an icon. The tooltip text can just be the button text.

So that's what I did. I've designed my website to consider users not having JavaScript enabled, so there is a hyperlink for each feed that a user can right click to select copy link. The "Copy Link" buttons rely on JavaScript, so they are hidden with a class of noscript until JavaScript is detected. Despite the sin of styling my buttons to look like hyperlinks, I really do care about accessibility, and I try to make sure the text to a button is indicative of the task it performs. I've also added aria-labels as the buttons all read the same text, and an aria-live attribute set to assertive - which changes to off while it waits for the timeout to reset the text. I've included a data-copytext property so I can avoid navigating between siblings to get data in the JavaScript.

<h2>Latest</h2>
<a href="/feed">https://aaronwatts.dev/feed</a>

<button 
  class="noscript"
  aria-label="Copy link for latest articles RSS feed"
  aria-live="assertive"
  data-copytext="https://aaronwatts.dev/feed"
>Copy Link</button>

<p>Latest articles from all categories.</p>

Thanks to the simple design the JavaScript is minimal. Once the DOM content has loaded, an init function unhides all the script dependent HTML elements, makes an array of all the copy buttons, then adds an event listener to each. In the event listener, the value collected from data-copytext is written to the clipboard, the buttons text content and aria live values are updated and the button is blurred from focus, and finally a timeout waits 3 seconds to reset the button back to its previous state.

document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init);

function init() {
  const noscript = document.querySelectorAll('.noscript');
  noscript.forEach(i => i.classList.remove('noscript'));

  const copyBtns = document.querySelectorAll('button[data-copytext]');

  copyBtns.forEach(btn => {
    btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
      const copyText = btn.dataset.copytext;
      
      navigator.clipboard.writeText(copyText);
      
      btn.textContent = "Link Copied!";
      btn.ariaLive = 'off';
      btn.blur();
      
      setTimeout(function() {
        btn.textContent = "Copy Link";
        btn.ariaLive = 'assertive';
      }, 3000);
    });
  });
}

I change the aria-live value to prevent screen readers from being interrupted when the text content gets reset - it doesn't really need a notification, but the feedback for the initial click is valuable. I'm not really sure if this is how it will play out in practise, but I hope that I've made a sensible UX pattern for everyone.

I'm still using an icon (with screenreader text) for the link to the RSS page, however RSS is niche and I expect that most people using it will know what the icon looks like. I'm not here to say you shouldn't be using icons and you are breaking the internet and that is very bad. But I do think it's worth appreciating how much simpler I was able to make things for myself by avoiding the aesthetically simple solution. Poetic! So next time you are considering doing the done thing, it might be worth asking: does the done thing need to be done?

item.title: Reading Times
item.description: Another day, another minor change to my website. I have added an estimated reading time to articles.
item.content:encoded:
Another day, another minor change to my website. I have added an estimated reading time to articles.

It wasn't a very complex addition. Just a line of PHP. I went with a lower reading speed, I'm a slow reader and I make guides which are slower to read than generic text. If you read faster than my site's estimated reading times, then pat yourself on the back.

<aside class="wpm">
  <p>
    <small>Estimated reading time: <?= ceil(str_word_count($content) / 200); ?> minutes</small>
  </p>
</aside>

I couldn't really decide where to fit it in to the flow of the document, so I just put it in before the main article as an aside. I think that's the correct way to use aside. MDN describes it as follows:

The <aside> HTML element represents a portion of a document whose content is only indirectly related to the document's main content. Asides are frequently presented as sidebars or call-out boxes.

But the only place I've really noticed them used in the wild is for adverts. I gave it a wpm class (words per minute). If only to set a specific margin on the reading times to push it down a bit from the top of the page, as the extra information was starting to feel a little cluttered.

The small inside the p element already has styling that suited the scenario. I think small works, it's not small print, but it's complimentary text that is not strictly necessary to the article itself - this is the way I use small elements for my side notes inside of articles. I had been using aside for side notes but I'm pretty sure that was wrong, so now it's small. Sometimes knowing the correct semantics in a particular situation is difficult.

I've been busy with other projects, so a small change that get's me near my blog for a moment is always welcome. I am always looking at improvements for this site of varying scale, which I'm sure I will get to soon. But for now, back to being busy elsewhere for a little while.

item.title: Pure Comments
item.description: Comments are back on my website! I had previously been using Cactus Comments to display comments from a Matrix room, but that project appears abandoned. I have a Coolify server now, so I can host a solution myself.
item.content:encoded:
Comments are back on my website! I had previously been using Cactus Comments to display comments from a Matrix room, but that project appears abandoned. I have a Coolify server now, so I can host a solution myself.

I'm using Pure Comments by Kev Quirk. Kev also makes other tools, which can be found on his Pure Commons website. I liked his Simple CSS "framework", and I'm in a position to learn some backend stuff now that I'm running my own Coolify instance, so I thought I'd give it a whirl.

I don't really promote my site. It's just a hobby and while I enjoy learning, I'm scared of being judged I guess. And the imposter syndrome - I am a hobbyist, so that shouldn't really bother me, but whatever .. it's fine. I'm not trying to get a job, I just like making things work. Either way, no one really left comments the last time I set it up, and maybe no one will again - but as I say I like making things that work, it's all fun for me.

I am quite proud of myself for getting this going. In the grand scheme of things I know very little about PHP and Linux servers, but I managed to brute force a Dockerfile to set up Pure Comments on an Apache server in a container. I couldn't get persistent storage working without locking the contents of a file, which is fine until you want to update the app settings. I'm not sure if I have made a misstep in setting up Coolify or not, or if that's just how it works. Pure Comments uses SQLite, which is a pain because now I'm going to have to rig up some kind of backup strategy for the comments unless I don't mind losing them all any time that the server is redeployed.

Apart from the pretty esoteric problems that I seem intent on creating for myself, Pure Comments is a breeze to get going. You will need to know how to set up a basic LAMP server, but after that it's idiot proof - and I should know. Once I got it working functionally, it was time for some styling. Or, de-styling in my case. Kev offers a default-come-example CSS file for Pure Comments. I wanted something quick so I started with his defaults, then made some changes to fit with my sites theming. My website has some terminal tropes, and the rest of it is intentionally simple, celebrating the old web with (close to) default colours, buttons that look like hyperlinks, and semantic HTML. Or am I just lazy.. So that meant going through the comments CSS file and quite literally roughing up any of the polish. Now my comments section looks as lazily designed as the rest of my website - and I like that!

item.title: Search Feature For Static Websites
item.description: I've just added a search feature to this website. The website is static, but it is built programmatically. After switching my build process over to a PHP one, the process of adding a search feature was actually pretty simple. It doesn't require PHP, you just need a way to set up a JSON object with the content you want to make searchable. I'll go over how I did it in this post.
item.content:encoded:
I've just added a search feature to this website. The website is static, but it is built programmatically. After switching my build process over to a PHP one, the process of adding a search feature was actually pretty simple. It doesn't require PHP, you just need a way to set up a JSON object with the content you want to make searchable. I'll go over how I did it in this post.

There are a few ways to achieve this. Google offer a programmable search engine if you have a static site that you want to make searchable but aren't very technically adept, or just want it done quickly. I don't want large scripts or services I don't control in my website so that's a no for me. Apache offer Solr if you want to host your own search index. I might return to look at this once I have a bit more experience setting up Docker images on my Coolify instance, and if the data collection on my website becomes so large that static searching becomes impractical. And then there's static searching; indexing the data within the client itself, and offloading the work to the users browser.

I want my site to work well and do it fast. So that had some influence on how I executed the process, and on which search tool I chose. Two standouts were FlexSearch and MiniSearch. But I went with Lunr, which was just easier to get going with a static file that I can keep on my own site. There are comments floating around StackOverflow pointing out that the project hasn't had an update since 2020, but since I'm not using NodeJS here, and the script itself appears safe, it shouldn't cause any issues.

Getting Started

First and foremost, we need the data we want to search. I used PHP for this and simply write the return value into a JSON file in my build script. I will also want to manipulate DOM to show results, so I will include a few extra bits to help with that.

<?php

$configs = include CONFIG_PATH . 'config.php';
require APP_PATH . 'helpers.php';
$posts = [];
$jsonResponse = array();

foreach ($configs['blogs'] as $blog => $blogDesc) {
    $posts += [...getBlogPosts($blog)];
}

foreach ($posts as $path => $post) {
  $content = getPostText($post['dom']);
  $postInfo = getPostInfo($post['dom']);
  [
    'title' => $title,
    'description' => $description,
    'date' => $date
  ] = $postInfo;


  $jsonResponse[$path] = [
    'url' => $path,
    'blog' => ucfirst($post['blog']),
    'textContent' => trim($content),
    'title' => $title,
    'description' => $description,
    'date' => $date,
    'dateString' => formatDate($date)
  ];
}
     
header('Content-Type: application/json;');
echo json_encode($jsonResponse);

This is the controller for my search/feed route in my static site generator. There's a few helper functions here doing most of the work with regard to organising the data, but essentially I'm just collecting the posts from all my blogs, getting a stripped down version of the text (I'm only including text within p elements and ignoring all else), getting a few helpful DOM extractions, and then sending that data in a JSON response, in the form of an array of objects. Writing that to a file is one line in the terminal, or a line in my BASH build script.

php index.php "search/feed" > dist/search/feed.json

Setting Up Search

How you execute the process is entirely up to you. I opted to keep it simple, and delegate as little work to the client as I could get away with while still having a functional search feature. I also plan for JavaScript to be disabled by the user or not to load. Here is a mildly entertaining post listing reasons why that might happen; the train tunnel phenomenon is something I occasionally experience as my commute to work goes underground a few times en route. So I went with a search form on the home page, which is hidden until the clients browser detects JavaScript, that directs a query to a search page where the search is actually executed.

<search id="search" class="noscript">
  <form action="/search">
    <input type="text" name="query" required placeholder="Search posts...">
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
  </form>
</search>

That snippet is actually a PHP partial that I can require in my home page and my search page. So later I can make changes to one block of code and have it persist wherever it is used.

Next we need the actual lunr file itself. The full static file can be found in the projects GitHub, and the guide offers an unpkg CDN file, but it's the full file, which is quite large. It's very well documented using JSDoc comments. I haven't seen it mentioned in the guide, but there is a minified version available from the unpkg CDN too. So I downloaded that straight into my project's files.

curl -o assets/scripts/lunr.js https://unpkg.com/lunr@2.3.9/lunr.min.js

Next, after including the script in the search page, we just need to fetch our JSON feed and build an index. There are extras available such as match indices and fuzzy search, but I explained in my blog why I opted to just use the defaults. So with the following in our own search.js we are ready to get started with setting up the rest of the page's functionality.

async function getFeed(url) {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(url);
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Response status: ${response.status}`);
    }

    const result = await response.json();

    return result;
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(error.message);
    return null;
  }
}
  
function getIdx(feed) {
  const idx = lunr(function () {
    this.ref('url');
    this.field('title');
    this.field('textContent');
    
    for (const item in feed) {
      this.add(feed[item]);
    }
  })

  return idx;
}
  
// perform a search
const feed = await getFeed('/search/feed.json');
const idx = getIdx(feed);
const results = idx.search(query);

Setting Up The Page Functionality

I've gotten into the habit of using classes when a bunch of code works together to achieve a single concept. Such as searching content. So I will be using a JavaScript class, while not telling you that OOP will change your life. If you prefer to work functionally, you will likely be passing a lot more parameters into functions if you aren't scoping globally (oops! Sorry, I literally just said I wouldn't do that).

Before we write any more script let's arrange our HTML first. We need the search form, and somewhere to put the results. I've chosen not to list results in an unordered list, but to present them as articles with links as I would in a blog page, so I'm breaking one of my own rules in this case and actually using a div element.

<search id="search" class="noscript">
  <form action="/search">
    <input type="text" name="query" required placeholder="Search posts...">
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
  </form>
</search>    

<div id="results" class="noscript">
  <h2></h2>
  
  <template id="result">
    <article>
      <header>
        <h3><a href=""></a></h3>
        <time></time>
      </header>
      <p class="description"></p>
      <a href="">Read More</a>
    </article>
  </template>
</div>

I've recently read a pretty good article about memory efficient DOM manipulation, so I'm going to be using a template element for my individual search results. Now that we have a DOM, it's time to write some JavaScript. It's also worth noting the noscript class attached to both elements here. They will be set to display: none in CSS until JavaScript is detected.

class Search {
  constructor(feed, idx) {
    this.feed = feed;
    this.idx = idx;
    
    this.resultsElem = document.querySelector('#results');
    this.form = this.document.querySelector('search#search form');
    this.template = results.querySelector('template#result');

    this.domMap = new WeakMap();
  }
}

Starting with just the constructor function for a class of Search, we can pass in the feed and index that we have already defined. In terms of DOM, we will want access to the results div, the search form, and the predefined template. I've also put a WeakMap instance in there, as the DOM will be being created and destroyed on consecutive searches, and a weak map ensures that removed elements are cleared by the garbage collector and don't stick around in memory. The form will need an event listener with preventDefault to prevent page loads when new searches are performed. I like to take care of this in an init method once I know everything is properly set up.

class Search {
  ...  

  init() {
    this.form.addEventListener('submit', evt => {
      evt.preventDefault();
      
      if (this.form.query.value.length > 0) {
        const query = this.form.query.value;
        const url = new URL(window.location);
        
        url.searchParams.set('query', query);
        history.pushState(null, '', url);
        
        this.form.query.value = '';
        document.activeElement.blur();
        
        this.results = this.handleSearch(query);
      }
    });
  } 
}

We prevent the default form action, and an arrow function preserves the this of the class, instead of referring to the event target as it would with a normal function callback. The DOM form object saves us a little work here, and we can ignore the form submission if the forms query value is empty. I set the search params on the url and push them to the history object, this allows the page to operate normally, and the user can cycle back through their previous searches, even though we are preventing page loads on form submission. Next the input value is set back to blank and the elements focus removed, before passing the query into a handleSearch method. Let's write that method now.

class Search {
  ...

  handleSearch(query) {
    this.removeResults();
    
    const results = this.idx.search(query);
    this.populate = this.populateResults(results);
    
    const msg = `Showing ${results.length} results for "${query}"`;
    this.resultsElem.querySelector('h2').textContent = msg;
  }  
}

The handleSearch method calls a removeResults method to remove any search results currently being displayed in the DOM, then performs a search with the provided query. The results are passed into a populateResults method to add them to the DOM. Finally a message is passed into the h2 element of the results div to explain to the user just what they are looking at exactly.

class Search {
  ...

  removeResults() {
    const results = this.resultsElem.querySelectorAll('article');
    results.forEach(i => i.remove());
  }
 
}

The removeResults method is quite simple, yet also quite powerful when combined with the weak map instance we defined in the constructor. It requires that elements are set in to the weak map first, as we will do in the populateResults method. But essentially it will strip all removed elements from memory via the garbage collector.

class Search {
  ...
  
  populateResults(results) {
    for (const result of results) {
      const post = this.feed[result['ref']];
      const url = post['url'] + '/';
     
      const clone = document.importNode(this.template.content, true);
      this.domMap.set(clone);
      
      const h3 = clone.querySelector('h3 > a');
      h3.textContent = `${post['title']} [${post['blog']}]`;
      h3.href = url;
      const timeEl = clone.querySelector('time');
      timeEl.textContent = post['dateString'];
      timeEl.dateTime = post['date'];
      clone.querySelector('p.description').textContent = post['description'];
      clone.querySelector('article > a').href = url;

      this.resultsElem.appendChild(clone);
    }
  } 
}

The populateResults method iterates through the results, while matching the referenced text to the post it was extracted from. It clones the template we defined in the HTML, and adds it to the weak map instance. Then it simply completes the required DOM and appends the newly created article element to the results div.

Since the getIdx and getFeed functions are purely concerned with the search feature, I will move them into the class as well, as static methods, so that they can be executed before an instance is created - since we can't create an instance until we have the data that they both return.

class Search{
...
  static async getFeed(url) {
    try {
      const response = await fetch(url);
      if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Response status: ${response.status}`);
      }

      const result = await response.json();

      return result;
    } catch (error) {
      console.log(error.message);
      return null;
    }
  }


  static getIdx(feed) {
    const idx = lunr(function () {
      this.ref('url');
      this.field('title');
      this.field('textContent');
      
      for (const item in feed) {
        this.add(feed[item]);
      }
    })

    return idx;
  }
}

Now everything is set up, we can set up the page controls. Since we are working with DOM, I like to use the DOMContentLoaded event to ensure the script has access to everything it needs upon execution.

document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', async function() {
  const feedUrl = '/search/feed.json';
  const feed = await Search.getFeed(feedUrl);

  if (feed !== null) {
    const idx = Search.getIdx(feed);
    const search = new Search(feed, idx);
    search.init();

  } else {
    const msg = 'Something went wrong, try reloading...';
    document.querySelector('#results h2').textContent = msg;
  }

  document.querySelectorAll('.noscript').forEach(i => {
    i.classList.remove('noscript');
  });
});

Once DOM content has loaded, the feed is fetched. If a feed is returned, instead of the null value that is triggered in the catch statement, then an index is created, and both values get passed into a new instance of Search which is then initialised to apply the search forms event listener. The noscript classes aren't removed until everything else has executed, so if something hangs and blocks the script, the page remains blank. Otherwise, if there's an error, a message will be displayed to the user that something has gone wrong.

URL Based Search Queries

We have a working search page, but we aren't quite finished. We haven't yet accounted for searches performed on the home page that are then routed to the search page via the form's action. Luckily, with the search instance, we have everything we need to achieve this in just a few lines of code.

if (feed !== null) {
  const idx = Search.getIdx(feed);
  const search = new Search(feed, idx);
  search.init();

  const searchParams = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search);
  
  if (searchParams.size > 0) {
    const query = searchParams.get('query');
    search.handleSearch(query);
  }
}

Using the URLSearchParams object, it is simple to pass in the window objects location information, and use that to extract the query and perform a search with the handleSearch method we defined earlier. The method will take care of everything for us including the DOM manipulation.

item.title: My Site Has a Search Feature
item.description: Now my website is running it's development environment and building it's static files using PHP, the process of making modifications has become much easier and more fluid. Because of this, I decided to I would explore the idea of implementing a search feature for my static site. And after about a days work, I now have a search feature!
item.content:encoded:
Now my website is running it's development environment and building it's static files using PHP, the process of making modifications has become much easier and more fluid. Because of this, I decided to I would explore the idea of implementing a search feature for my static site. And after about a days work, I now have a search feature!

When I started researching the idea, I didn't expect it to be quite so .. easy. A quick web search landed me on a recommendation for lunr.js, followed immediately by a warning saying it hasn't been updated since around 2020. I looked around elsewhere, but I came back to take a second look at lunr. It had a frontend JavaScript file I could just download and use, everything else seemed to require Node JS or a CDN script. I'm doing my best to try and keep this project out of the Node JS ecosystem, and external CDN's are a no for me as I want everything in the same place - if the script isn't loading then it's likely that the website won't either, removing the risk of broken dependencies. I suppose I could curl the CDN script into a file, but most other solutions I looked at provide minified versions which are difficult to audit.

So I came back to lunr. I perused the source file just to make sure it wasn't connecting to any external services on the sly (it doesn't), and that was good enough for me. The scariest thing about it is that it uses the old pseudoclass functions - so archaic! The website doesn't make it clear, but there is minified version of the cdn script that can lighten the load since the main script is very well documented - I could learn a thing or two there I guess. So after a curl -o lunr.js https://unpkg.com/lunr@2.3.9/lunr.min.js I was ready to go.

I'm pretty happy with the result. I enjoyed working on it so much that I may do a guide in the near future. I've deployed the changes and eveything seems to be working fine so far. For it to work I had to generate a JSON feed with the text from all the posts across my site, and some additional data to build the DOM. The file is a little heavy at 168.9kB - more than any other file on my website but I'd argue that it's still perfectly acceptable. The JetBrains woff file isn't too far behind at 113.7kB - maybe I should look at a few other ligature monospace fonts? The JSON feed was easy enough to generate with PHP, and of course it's deployed from a static file so it's only ever my machine doing the work prior deployment with regard to the PHP code.

There were some upgrade options, such as fuzzy search and returning indices of the matches. But after experimenting, I decided fuzzy search returns far too many matches for "raspberry pi" - by default it tokenises the query, and pi with a fuzz setting of just 1 becomes far too lenient. The indices might have been helpful if the text samples were smaller. I don't imagine it being too difficult to iterate backwards through the string indices and plug in some mark tags to highlight the matches, but my text samples are just too large so it's not worth it. So I just stuck with the defaults, and I'm just presenting my results as I would a list of posts in any of the blog feeds, albeit without the option to filter topics.

item.title: My Path From Here
item.description: I've been finding time to spend coding recently. I've learned a little PHP and applied it. My energy is high, but my focus and direction are low.
item.content:encoded:
I've been finding time to spend coding recently. I've learned a little PHP and applied it. My energy is high, but my focus and direction are low.

I suppose that this is a post just to keep me mentally on track. I've found time, against the odds, to learn a little PHP and apply it. That's got me excited to be at my computer again. I also migrated my site over to my Coolify server. Migrating and changing my build tools also meant I had to fix a few bugs that slipped through in all the excitement. I also made some quality of life changes to my website, and dusted off an old checklist of a few things I wanted to implement but never got round to, and ticked those all off too.

So I'm here because I started learning PHP. And now my enthusiasm is high but not pointed anywhere in particular, so I'm doing that thing where I get pulled toward anything I find remotely interesting. Distractions. Carry on with PHP - if just the syntax got me this excited then I ought to force myself back on track and keep going.

item.title: Unicorns
item.description: I got unicorns. I've seen a few people raging at GitHub lately, I don't like joining in on politics. But my personal website has been affected now and I've taken action.
item.content:encoded:
I got unicorns. I've seen a few people raging at GitHub lately, I don't like joining in on politics. But my personal website has been affected now and I've taken action.

I'm not leaving GitHub. Not yet anyway. If I did I would most likely move everything over to my GitLab account - I haven't even logged into it for years, but it exists. I've heard a lot of opinions that GitLab is just as bad (as GitHub), but I don't see self-hosting repositories as a solution for me. I already host my own NextCloud and Coolify instances, I can't imagine looking after a versioning hosting server - I am managing my cloud and web server, but I often feel a little out of my depth in doing so. Also, code repositories are something I would prefer not lose - and I'd like the liberty of being able to blame someone else if something were to happen to them.

So, for now, I am still hosting the repository for this website on GitHub, but it's now deployed through my Coolify instance. I had considered moving it to my Netlify account, but Netlify has lambdas, so I would prefer to keep that for projects that require a little more functionality than a standard static website, but don't necessarily require a proper server. There are, of course, other services, but I already have so many accounts for so many things, so I'm making use of what I already have set up for now.

The unicorns. I had heard about them, but not seen them myself. Until a few months ago. If the GitHub servers go down proper, you see the unicorn. It's something to do with their server using software called Unicorn. But I've now adopted the phrase for whenever GitHub doesn't work. The first unicorn was when I tried to make a commit a little while ago, and it wasn't working. So I did a DuckDuckGo search for how to test my GitHub SSH connection to make sure that it was working correctly. The GitHub page with the instructions failed, as did the rest of the website, and there was the majestic creature right on my screen. Yesterday, I commited a new post to my blog, and the GitHub Pages action kept timing out after a few seconds. I couldn't figure out what was wrong. I have a strong suspicion that I'm nowhere near any of the size limits imposed on the free GitHub Pages websites. Furthermore, it was a brand new repository with hardly any history as I had just changed my website management tool to a new one that I had written in PHP to replace my old Python one. There's been speculation that A.I. agents have been reeking havoc on GitHubs servers. Whatever the reason, it might have been fine if I had just waited a few hours, but I do a lot of work on that particular repository and I don't want to have to wait a day to push an update.

Moving the project over to Coolify wasn't too difficult. The NixPacks set up is pretty simple. I can serve from the dist folder now too, which is nice. There were ways to do that with GitHub Pages, but it was just easier to go with the default docs directory and not have to use custom actions. For the site to redeploy on pushes I had to set up a webhook in GitHub, hopefully that is less taxing on their servers than the Github Pages action, and therefore less likely to cause issues later on. Getting the DNS moved over wasn't too tricky either, although I had forgotten what I was doing with the CloudFlare tunnel as it doesn't come up as an option on the DNS configuration page (Coolify is running on a Raspberry Pi on my desk so the usual point at IP and go won't suffice here). I did eventually find it again in the zero trust section, and after copying the values I had set for *.aaronwattts.dev over to aaronwatts.dev, it was just a case of waiting for the new settings to propogate.

So now my website is self-hosted - which is cool, I guess. I've changed the powered by in the footer from GtitHub Pages to Raspberry Pi. They are quite concise about the use of their logo so that's one less SVG for me to worry about. The terms of use apparently apply to the words "Raspberry Pi" too, but I'll risk it, I'm an avid fan of their work and you'll be pressed to find a bad word about them on this website.

item.title: PHP Template Partials
item.description: This won't be long enough to make it into the guides section of my site. But from enquiring with search engines, I couldn't find an answer that gave an answer that was quite complex compared to how a partial normally works, or showed how to do PHP partials with X framework. So I'm including in my blog as a note.
item.content:encoded:
This won't be long enough to make it into the guides section of my site. But from enquiring with search engines, I couldn't find an answer that gave an answer that was quite complex compared to how a partial normally works, or showed how to do PHP partials with X framework. So I'm including in my blog as a note.

I was having trouble working out how to include partials in my PHP templates. But this morning I had that well, duh! moment and rigged some up for my website. The same way I require a template, I just needed to require the partial within the template itself. So now I can make adjustments to things like my footer once, and not have to worry about consistency across pages.

<!-- header.php -->
<header>
  <h1>Welcome to my website!</h1>
</header>

<!-- index.php -->
<html>
  <body>
    <?php require PARTIALS_PATH . 'header.php' ?>
  </body>
</html>
